Before you start

Each slide carries its own point, so you can talk with the room instead of reading notes. Putting things off is about avoiding a feeling, so keep laziness out of it. Nobody names the task they are avoiding. If a student seems stuck on everything for weeks, connect them with a counselor.

Every student in the room

For students with ADHD willpower talk makes it worse, and "put the phone in another room" assumes another room, so a bag or a drawer works too.

If you want more

The full plan, care notes, and research. None of it is needed to teach the lesson.

Lesson plan

A suggested plan. Change the timing, skip or reorder slides, or use any part on its own. You know your students.

Goal

Students can explain procrastination as avoiding a feeling (short-term mood repair), see why "I work better under pressure" backfires, and leave with one if-then plan for a real task they've been putting off. The aim is a method. Nobody should leave thinking they're lazy.

Materials

  • The deck on the big screen. Each slide carries its own point, so no script is needed.
  • The take-home link to share after the talk

Flow

  1. 8 minFour myths, one per slide
  2. 6 minThe avoidance loop, and dodging a feeling
  3. 5 minWhat do you do instead? Turn and talk, share out
  4. 4 minUnder pressure: who was more stressed by the end?
  5. 4 minFour levers
  6. 10 minWhich lever? Jordan, Nina, Marcus
  7. 3 minIf-then plans
  8. 5 minEvery student, where else this shows up, close

Short on time (20-minute advisory)

Two myths, the avoidance loop, the pressure question, the four levers, one stuck student, and an if-then plan.

Before you teach
Treat it as a feeling problem.

Most students have been told procrastination means they're lazy or don't care. Start from the research: people put things off to escape a bad feeling. Students who feel seen will listen. Students who feel judged will tune out.

Keep what they're avoiding private.

Don't ask anyone to say what they've put off, how far behind they are, or what grade they got. The if-then plan stays with the student. The pair-share is only the time and place, never the task.

Skip the phone lecture.

The phone study is useful. A sermon about screens costs you the room. Keep it to friction: where the phone sits while you work.

Be honest about the research.

Most of these studies were with college students, and Steel's motivation equation is a simplified model. Say so. Students trust you more for it.

When it's more than procrastination.

A student who can't start things in most classes, no matter what they try, or who has always struggled with time and finishing, may have ADHD or another learning difference. Connect them with the learning specialist or a counselor.

When mood is the bigger problem.

If a student says avoiding work comes with feeling anxious, flat or hopeless most days, or that they're so far behind catching up feels impossible, thank them and walk them to a counselor that day. Don't work through it in front of the class.

Every student in the room

Culture, family, identity, ability and money: what to keep in mind for this topic.

ADHD and executive function.

For students with ADHD, starting is often the hardest part, and willpower talk makes it worse. If-then plans, timers and adding friction are the same tools that help them most. Avoid diagnoses as casual adjectives ("I'm so ADHD today") in your own examples.

Time after school isn't equal.

Some students work, ride a long bus, or watch younger siblings or cousins until an adult gets home. Nina's scenario has this in it. Short sprints and a 10-minute first step fit a tight evening. Every tool in this lesson is free.

"Put the phone in another room" assumes another room.

Some students share a bedroom or study at the kitchen table. A bag, a drawer, a friend holding it, or app timers all add the same friction.

The person who asks can be anyone.

"Tell someone who'll ask about it" works with a grandparent, an older sibling, a coach, a friend on a call, or a foster parent. Don't assume a parent is home to check.

Some students carry extra weight on a hard task.

The brain flags a hard task as a threat to your image or your sense of being smart. A student who is first in their family at a school like this, or new to it, may feel that threat more. Name it as common and keep the reflection private.

Language and "I don't get the assignment."

For a student learning English, "I don't understand what they want" is a real reason a task feels impossible to start. Asking the teacher counts as a first step. A bad first draft can start in any language.

What the research says

Procrastination is choosing short-term mood repair over long-term goals: avoiding how the task makes you feel.

Sirois and Pychyl, Social and Personality Psychology Compass, 2013

Combining hundreds of studies, one model of motivation: confidence times value, divided by impulsiveness times delay. Simplified, it shows four places to push.

Steel, Psychological Bulletin, 2007

College procrastinators felt less stressed early in the semester. By the end they were more stressed, got sick more often and earned lower grades.

Tice and Baumeister, Psychological Science, 1997

Students who forgave themselves for procrastinating before one exam procrastinated less before the next.

Wohl, Pychyl and Bennett, Personality and Individual Differences, 2010

A review of 94 studies found if-then plans (when, where and what, decided ahead) meaningfully increase follow-through.

Gollwitzer and Sheeran, Advances in Experimental Social Psychology, 2006

Students did worse on attention and memory tasks with their phone on the desk, face down and silent, than with it in another room.

Ward et al., Journal of the Association for Consumer Research, 2017

In brain scans, thinking about yourself ten years from now looks more like thinking about another person than about yourself.

Ersner-Hershfield et al., Social Cognitive and Affective Neuroscience, 2009

People who struggle most to act on their intentions showed weaker links between the amygdala and the anterior cingulate, which helps the planner step in.

Schlüter et al., Psychological Science, 2018
